records.name: West Philly Insight
records.summary: A free weekly meditation group in West Philadelphia, open to anyone, that meets at Calvary Community Center on Baltimore Avenue.
records.what_you_do: Sit with the group in the Insight style, and join the Saturday guided meditation and talk or a weekday sit.

schedule.text: Saturdays 1 to 2 pm: guided meditation and a talk, open to all. Wednesdays: two half hour sits, 7 to 7:30 am and 7:35 to 8:05 am, open to all. Thursdays: two half hour sits, 7 to 7:30 pm and 7:35 to 8:05 pm, listed for BIPOC.

cost.text: Classes are offered freely. No donation policy is stated.

access.notes: The meeting room is up a flight of stairs from the Baltimore Avenue door. The page does not mention an elevator.

first_step.how: Come to the Saturday 1 to 2 pm session at Calvary Community Center, 4740 Baltimore Ave, or email the group to ask about the weekday sits.
first_step.basis: The sits are open to all and the page invites questions by email, but it does not say whether you need to register first.
first_step.what_to_expect: The Saturday session runs about an hour: a guided meditation, then a talk and time for questions, then tea. The weekday sits are two 30 minute sits, and you can come to one or both. The classes are free, and the page lists no fee or donation.
first_visit_tips: Use the red double doors on Baltimore Avenue, and look for the chalkboard sign out front.
Climb the stairs on your left after the door, and the room is at the top.
Cushions, blankets and yoga mats are kept in a glass cabinet in the room.

records.notes: The schedule page is the group's own and is current: it lists a daylong retreat on October 10, 2026, which is the last sign of life. The Thursday sits are labeled For BIPOC and start September 24 (no year shown on the page). One of three reads of that page did not show the label, so please check it by eye before publishing. The site has no parking or transit details. Drop in and sign up are not stated, so they are left out.

records.name: West Philly Runners
records.summary: A West Philadelphia running club with a weekly group run in 2, 4 or 6 mile options and a Monday speed workout. It welcomes runners of many paces.
records.what_you_do: Join the Wednesday night group run at your pace, or the Monday speed workout if you want to train harder.

schedule.text: Wednesday night group run from Clark Park, with a 2, 4 or 6 mile choice. Monday speed workout at 6:30 pm in Penn Park. Friday coffee run at 6:30 am from Clark Park.

first_step.how: Go to Clark Park for the Wednesday night group run and choose a 2, 4 or 6 mile loop, or subscribe for weekly run news on the club's site.
first_step.basis: The site invites beginners and experienced runners alike, names where the Wednesday run starts, and asks you to subscribe for weekly news. It does not say whether you must sign up before a run.
first_step.what_to_expect: The Wednesday run starts at Clark Park and finishes at a local bar, and you pick a 2, 4 or 6 mile route. The club says all paces are welcome, though most runners keep at least a 12-minute pace. The site does not give a start time or a cost for the regular run.
first_visit_tips: Clark Park, at 44th and Baltimore Avenue, is where the Wednesday run starts.
Pick your distance before you start: 2, 4 or 6 miles.
The Monday speed workout is at 6:30 pm in Penn Park if you want more speed work.

records.notes: Cost, drop in and sign up are not on the site, so they are left out. The upcoming events page lists a run titled What the El 2026 on October 17 (the title shows the year), which starts at Frankford Transportation Center and suggests a donation to Prevention Point Philadelphia. It is a one time event, so it is not in schedule.text. The October 14 event page shows an unlabeled 1:30 PM time under the date; we did not use it as a start time. The Friday coffee run appears only on the about page. The Wednesday start time is not stated.

records.name: Wild Hand
records.summary: A fiber shop in Mount Airy with classes in knitting, crochet, weaving and spinning. It runs a free weekly Fiber Folk Night on Wednesday evenings from 5 to 7 pm.
records.what_you_do: Come to Fiber Folk Night on a Wednesday, or sign up for a beginner class such as community knit or crochet basics.

schedule.text: Fiber Folk Night every Wednesday from 5 to 7 pm, free. The shop also lists beginner classes in knitting, crochet, weaving and spinning, and some are for kids.

cost.text: Fiber Folk Night is free. Single classes run from about $10 for the community basics up to $100, and two day retreats cost $350.

access.notes: The shop is wheelchair accessible, but its own restroom is not. The neighboring High Point Cafe has an accessible restroom that customers may use. Nearest SEPTA: the Chestnut Hill West Regional Rail line, at the Upsal or Carpenter Lane stop, about a 10 minute walk.

requirements.gear: Bring your own fiber project to Fiber Folk Night.

first_step.how: Come to Fiber Folk Night on a Wednesday from 5 to 7 pm at 606 Carpenter Lane, bringing a project to work on. For a class, open the class page from the Workshops list on the shop's site and sign up there.
first_step.basis: Fiber Folk Night is free, walk-ins are fine, and the page says first timers and people still learning are welcome. Beginner classes are also listed, but the site does not describe a separate newcomer program.
first_step.what_to_expect: Fiber Folk Night is a weekly, free evening where people bring their own fiber project and work on it alongside others, from knitting and crochet to spinning. Everyone is welcome at any skill level, and you can walk in without signing up. The page does not say whether tables and seating are provided.
first_visit_tips: Bring a project you can work on, since the page asks visitors to bring one.
There is no lot, but free street parking is usually within one block.
Check the shop's email and social media for last minute changes.

records.notes: The site has no dated news with a year, so status stays probably_active. Class dates on the site show no year and are not used. The site does not say whether class materials are included. The 5 to 7 pm time comes from the homepage; the Fiber Folk Night product page gives no times.

records.name: Wildflower Composers
records.summary: A mentoring program for early-career composers who are women, transgender, nonbinary or genderqueer. It runs a summer festival each July at Temple University and offers six-week online mini-courses.
records.what_you_do: Apply to the summer festival if you are 13 to 19, take an online mini-course, or come to the free premiere concert each July. The site also lists a lab and a resident composer placement.

schedule.text: The festival runs each July on the Temple University campus. Six-week online mini-courses meet weekly on Zoom at set times; in 2025 they met on Monday and Wednesday evenings.

cost.text: Festival tuition is $900, and dorm room and board is $1,400 more for students who stay on campus. There is no application fee, and financial aid, including full scholarships, is available. Each online mini-course is $200.

first_step.how: If you are 13 to 19, read the festival page and apply while admissions are open, which is until spots fill. Adults can ask about the mini-courses by emailing erin@wildflowercomposers.org.
first_step.basis: Entry is by application. The festival and the mini-courses both take applications, and the mini-course page does not describe the application steps.
first_step.what_to_expect: The festival runs about two weeks in July on the Temple University campus. Students take daily seminars and private composition lessons with a mentor, workshop a piece with Network for New Music musicians, and write a new piece that is premiered on the last day. Tuition is $900, plus room and board for students who live on campus, and the premiere concert is free and open to the public.
first_visit_tips: The final premiere concert at Rock Hall is free and needs no advance registration, so you can hear what the festival makes.
Chaperones walk students between buildings at all times.
Tell the program about any dietary restrictions or allergies, which it says it can accommodate.

records.notes: The festival page gives 2026 dates (July 6 to 17). The events page lists a faculty concert on July 8, 2026 under past events, which is the last sign of life. Tier 1 described the festival as in person or online; the festival page says it is on campus, and online mini-courses are separate, so the summary was corrected. Festival students must be 13 to 19 and not already in a four-year degree; the mini-courses have no maximum age. The mini-course page still lists only 2025 courses and says to check back next year, so no 2026 mini-course dates are given. Admissions are open until filled; spot counts are not recorded because they change. The premiere concert on the events page shows July 17 with no year next to it.

records.name: WINC Tradeswomen Readiness Program
records.summary: A six week pre-apprenticeship for women who want skilled jobs in construction, manufacturing or transit. It builds safety, math and job skills and helps with applications.
records.what_you_do: Take safety training, build math and job skills, learn about the trades, and get ready to apply for apprenticeships.

schedule.text: Six week cohorts, held Tuesday through Thursday from 8 am to 4:30 pm.

first_step.how: Use the Apply Now link at womenbuildpa.org, or email winc@fti.edu or call 267-939-0035 to ask about the next cohort.
first_step.basis: You apply first, and the program lists requirements before you start: age 18 or older, a valid driver's license, a high school diploma or GED, and passing a drug test.
first_step.what_to_expect: This is a six week pre-apprenticeship, with classes Tuesday through Thursday from 8 am to 4:30 pm at the Finishing Trades Institute on Horning Road. Training covers safety, education, mentorship and help with job applications, and you explore trades such as carpentry, welding, HVAC and painting. Orientation sessions are held in person, and the site does not say whether taking part costs anything.
first_visit_tips: Check the listed requirements first: 18 or older, a valid driver's license, a high school diploma or GED, and passing a drug test.
Philadelphia residents get priority in the program.
Orientation sessions are held in person at the training site, so plan to go there.

records.notes: The program's own site (womenbuildpa.org) is now the website. It describes the Women in Nontraditional Careers (WINC) Trade Readiness Pre-Apprenticeship, run with the Finishing Trades Institute; the PhilaWorks page has less detail. The site banner and FAQ say the next six-week cohort starts in October 2026; the PhilaWorks page did not show that on one read. Cost is not stated anywhere we read, so it is left out. Staff contacts on the program site: Erin O'Brien-Hofmann at 267-939-0035 and Keriann Madden at 215-900-1987. The 215-963-2100 number is the PhilaWorks office listed on the PhilaWorks page. Old news on that page is dated 2020 and 2022 and was not used for status.

records.name: Wissahickon East Park Friends
records.summary: A Friends group for Wissahickon East Park, listed by the City of Philadelphia. We have not yet confirmed what it does or when it meets.
records.what_you_do: Ask the City's stewardship office to connect you with the group. Friends groups usually organize park cleanups and plantings, but we have not confirmed what this one does.

first_step.how: Email the City's Parks and Recreation stewardship office at PPRstewardship@phila.gov, or call 215-683-3679, and ask to be connected with this Friends group.
first_step.basis: We could not confirm this group's own join or meeting steps. The only way in we found is through the City's stewardship office, so the way in is unclear.

records.notes: The site had no more detail than tier 1. The only public page the City lists is a Facebook page. Under the leads only rule we did not read it for facts, so activities, meeting times, cost and first visit are not known. Status changed from active to unknown: the only 2026 date was the City listing record date, which is not an event, post or notice. The treasurer's name from public tax data was dropped as personal detail. The owner may want to hold this record until the group confirms current activity.

records.name: Wissinoming Park
records.summary: The Friends of Wissinoming look after Wissinoming Park in Northeast Philadelphia. The last public report we found is a November 2023 fall cleanup, where volunteers planted trees and bulbs, raked, and picked up trash with the city and the Fairmount Park Conservancy.
records.what_you_do: Join park cleanups and planting days. The group has worked on these with the city and the Fairmount Park Conservancy.

first_step.how: Email the City's Parks and Recreation stewardship office at PPRstewardship@phila.gov, or call 215-683-3679, and ask to be connected with the Friends of Wissinoming.
first_step.basis: The group's own site did not open, so we could not confirm how to join. The only way in we found is through the City's stewardship office, so the way in is unclear.
first_step.what_to_expect: A November 2023 fall cleanup drew over 100 volunteers, who planted trees and bulbs, raked, mulched, swept and picked up trash before winter. We have no newer details on meeting times or cost.

records.notes: Both www.wissinomingpark.org and wissinomingpark.org failed to resolve (DNS), so the group's own site could not be read. The newest dated evidence is a Love Your Park recap dated November 17, 2023, so status is dormant under the 24 month rule. Tier 1 had active, based on the City list record date (2026-10); that is a listing date, not an event, post or notice, so it was not used. The website is kept from tier 1 but does not resolve. Please check whether the Friends are still active before publishing. One web search for this group found no contact details, meeting times or upcoming dates.
